blocks.title: <ico-book></ico-book> NEVER HAVE I…
blocks.intro: Put a negative or limiting word first, and the sentence turns around: the auxiliary jumps in front of the subject, as in a question. It is the sound of speeches, editorials and formal writing, and it works because it is rare.

vocab.sp: a piece that gives the opinion of the station or newspaper
the group of people elected to run a city
a building or place that everyone knows
to stop broadcasting; to become silent
to stay with them so they are not alone
to say publicly what you think

blocks.note: How it works: flashcards , rewrite , listening , gap-fill , compare and order . Press CHECK wherever you see it.

parts.html: 1 · WHAT MOVES — the auxiliary jumps before the subject

items.en: I have never seen such a crowd.
Never have I seen such a crowd.
items.sp: «Never» goes first, so have + I, exactly like a question.

parts.html: 2 · NO AUXILIARY? ADD DO, DOES, DID — again, like a question

items.en: Rarely does a station last fifty years.
items.sp: A station rarely lasts… → does + a station + last.

items.en: Little did they know that we were listening.
items.sp: They did not know at all… → did + they + know.

items.en: Not only does it inform the city, it also keeps it company.
items.sp: Only the first half is inverted.

parts.html: 3 · THE TIME PAIR — no sooner… than · hardly… when

items.en: No sooner had we gone on air than the lights went out.
items.sp: One thing happened immediately after the other. No sooner… than.

items.en: Hardly had the show started when the phone rang.

parts.html: 4 · ONLY WHEN, NOT UNTIL — the inversion waits for the second half

items.en: Only when the music stopped did we notice the silence.
items.sp: Not «did the music stop»: the main clause is the one that turns.

items.en: Not until midnight did the last caller hang up.
items.sp: The time phrase first, then did + subject.

parts.html: 5 · TWO MORE, AND A WARNING — under no circumstances · so… that

items.en: Under no circumstances should this studio close.
So loud was the applause that we stopped the show.
items.sp: So + adjective first, then be + subject.

parts.body: Register. Inversion is powerful once in a text. Twice is the limit. Three times is theater. In everyday conversation it sounds like a speech, so keep it for writing, presentations and moments that matter.

parts.html: SPANISH TRAP — «Nunca he visto…»: el español no da la vuelta

items.en: Never have I heard such nonsense.
items.sp: En español «Nunca he oído…» mantiene el orden. En inglés, con Never al principio, hay que invertir.

items.en: Not only did he come, he also stayed all night.
items.sp: «No solo vino…» → Not only did he come.
Aquí no hay inversión: only acompaña al sujeto, no abre una frase de tiempo o condición.

parts.body: Never I have seen this. → Never have I seen this. · Not only he came… → Not only did he come… · Only does Nora know. → Only Nora knows.

blocks.intro: Each card is a word that turns the sentence around. Try to build a sentence with it before you flip.

blocks.title: <ico-star></ico-star> THE HEADLINE
blocks.intro:
Bad news at the Radio Tower: the city council wants to close the rooftop studio. Nora will answer on air tonight with an editorial. Her first draft says «I have never been so proud of this station.» True, but flat. It needs a headline.

WORDS OF THE DAY (they must appear in your writing): a landmark = a place everyone knows · stand your ground · keep someone company.

cast.sp: has a sharp ear for mistakes

blocks.title: TURN IT AROUND
blocks.intro: Rewrite each flat sentence so that it starts with the words already in the box. Remember: the auxiliary goes before the subject.

items.source: I have never been prouder of this station.
answers: Never have I been prouder of this station.
Rarely do we hear good news.
items.why: No auxiliary in the original, so add do.

items.source: This studio should not close under any circumstances.
answers: Under no circumstances should this studio close.
items.why: should + this studio. The «not» is already inside «no».

items.source: They did not know that we were listening.
answers: Little did they know that we were listening.
Little did they know we were listening.

items.source: It not only informs the city, it also keeps it company.
answers: Not only does it inform the city, it also keeps it company.
Not only does it inform the city, but it also keeps it company.
Not only does it inform the city, it keeps it company.
Not only does it inform the city but also keeps it company.
items.why: does + it + inform: «informs» loses its -s. Only the first half turns.

items.source: The show had hardly started when the phone rang.
answers: Hardly had the show started when the phone rang.

items.source: We had no sooner gone on air than the lights went out.
answers: No sooner had we gone on air than the lights went out.

items.why: did + I + understand: the past moves to «did».

blocks.title: AUDIO 1 · THE EDITORIAL
blocks.desc: Nora on air, answering the council's plan to close the rooftop studio. Count the inversions: she uses each one exactly where it matters.

questions.q: What are Nora's three reasons for keeping the studio?
options: It is the only local newsroom, it is cheap to run, and it belongs to the listeners
It is old, it is famous, and it makes money for the city
It has the best view, the best hosts and the best music

questions.q: Which sentence carries her strongest demand?
options: Hundreds of you have written to us.
Under no circumstances should it go quiet.
It costs less than you think.

questions.q: Who is Nora really speaking to at the end?
options: The council members who will vote

questions.q: What does "Little did they know" introduce?
options: Something the council did not expect: the letter with four thousand names
Something the council had planned in secret
A fact about the fireworks budget

speaking.prompt: Read Nora's three inverted lines aloud, with a pause before each one: 'Never have I…', 'Not only does it…', 'Under no circumstances…'.
speaking.starter: Never have I been prouder of this station. Not only does it inform this city, it keeps it company. Under no circumstances should it go quiet.

transcript.html: Good evening. Tonight I'm not here to read the news. I'm here because of it. Last week, the city council announced a plan to close the rooftop studio of the Radio Tower, the room I am speaking from right now. They call it a saving. I'd like to tell you what it would cost.
Never have I been prouder of this station than in the last few days. Hundreds of you have written to us. Some of you have listened since before I was born.

Let me give you three reasons why this studio matters. First, it is the only local newsroom this city has left. Not only does it inform this city, it keeps it company. Ask anyone who works nights. Second, it costs less than you think: less per year than the council spends on fireworks. And third, it belongs to you. Your grandparents paid for this tower, brick by brick.
When the council met last Tuesday, they expected no one to notice. Little did they know that four thousand of you would sign a letter in three days.

So tonight I am speaking to the nine people who will vote next month. You have the numbers in front of you. Now you have the letters as well. Rarely does a city get the chance to keep something that still works. Under no circumstances should it go quiet.
I'm Nora. This is The Signal. And we are staying on the air.

blocks.title: WHICH AUXILIARY?
blocks.intro: Look at the verb form that follows the gap. It tells you which auxiliary can stand in front of the subject.

items.q: Never ___ I heard such a silence.
Rarely ___ a radio station last fifty years.
Little ___ they know that the microphone was on.
No sooner ___ we started than the power failed.
Under no circumstances ___ you touch that button.
Not only ___ she write the editorial, she also read it on air.
Only when the music stopped ___ we notice the noise.
Hardly had I sat down ___ the phone rang.

blocks.title: FLAT vs HEADLINE
blocks.intro: Same fact, same words. One is conversation; the other is a headline.

pair.a: I have never seen such a crowd.
pair.b: Never have I seen such a crowd.

items.q: Which would you say to a friend over coffee?
Which belongs in a speech or an editorial?
Apart from the position of "never", what changes in B?
options: The auxiliary comes before the subject
Rarely do we get a second chance.
Rarely we get a second chance.
Rarely we do get a second chance.
Only does Nora know the answer.

blocks.title: BUILD THE HEADLINE
blocks.intro: Tap the words in order. The trigger goes first, then the auxiliary, then the subject.

items.answer: Never have I seen such a crowd
Rarely does a city get a second chance
Under no circumstances should this studio close
Little did they know that we were listening
Only then did I understand the problem

blocks.title: AUDIO 2 · THE PROMOS
blocks.desc: Theo records three ten-second promos for tomorrow, and Roz listens. All three use inversion. One of them gets it wrong.

options: Not only we do bring you the news…
Not only bring we you the news…
Not only do we bring you the news…

questions.q: According to promo three, when does the real conversation begin?
How does Roz deal with the mistake?
options: She rewrites the line for Theo
She makes Theo hear it, and he fixes it himself

speaking.prompt: Record a ten-second promo for your own radio show, with one inversion and the time it is on.
speaking.starter: Never has… / Only when… does… / Not only do we…, we also… (Name of your show). (Day and time).

transcript.html: Okay, Theo, three promos for tomorrow. Ten seconds each. Promo one.
"Never has this city needed its radio more. The Signal. Tonight at nine."
"Not only we bring you the news, we bring you the people behind it. The Signal. Weeknights at nine."
Hmm. Something's off in that one. Read me promo three.
"Only when the city sleeps does the real conversation begin. The Signal. After midnight, with Theo."
I love that one. Now go back to promo two and listen to yourself. "Not only we bring."
Ah. "Not only do we bring you the news."
There it is. Record it again and we're done.

blocks.title: <ico-pen></ico-pen> MY EDITORIAL
blocks.intro: Something you care about is in danger: a park, a library, a tradition, a small business. Write a short editorial defending it (about 100 words).
checklist: Exactly two inversions, each one where it matters most
At least one with do / does / did (Rarely do we… / Not only does it…)
Two or three clear reasons, in plain word order
A strong last line (Under no circumstances should…)
The words of the day: a landmark, stand your ground, keep someone company
blocks.placeholder: Tonight I want to talk about…
blocks.example: what is in danger, and who wants to close it. Never have I past participle + how you feel. Let me give you two / three reasons. First, reason 1. Second, reason 2. reason 3, if you have one. Under no circumstances should subject + verb.
blocks.hw: Write your editorial, then record it as if you were on air: slow down before each inversion. Send me the text and the audio on WhatsApp.

rubric.d: About 100 words, and it is clear what you are defending, from whom, and why.
Exactly two inversions, both correctly formed (auxiliary before subject) and placed where they add force.
A listener follows it in one hearing. No word-for-word translation from Spanish.
